To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
caffeine-induced contraction is attenuated in diabetic rat aortas, but noradrenaline-induced contraction is not.
the contractile response of the aortic smooth muscle to noradrenalin is not impaired in diabetic rats, but that the contractile effect of caffeine is attenuated.

The ability of caffeine, which mobilizes Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), to induce phasic contractions in Ca2+-free medium is impaired in diabetic aorta, whereas the ability of noradrenaline, which mobilizes inositol 3,4,5 trisphosphate (IP3) from the ER, to induce phasic contractile response in Ca2+- free medium remains intact.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of streptozotcin diabetes on the contractile response of rat aorta to the agonists noradrenaline, angiotensin II, vasopressin and caffeine, in Ca(2+) -free and Ca(2+ +)-containing media, and the effects of the inhibitors of phospholipase C, U-73122 and neomycin, on the contractile responses.
the effect of diabetes on the contractile response of the rat thoracic aorta.
the study of the effects of diabetes on the contractile response of aorta to the alpha-adrenergic agonist, noradrenaline, and to the Ca(2+), mobilizing agent, caffeine.

caffeine is a more potent vasopressor than isoproterenol.
the impairment of Ca2+-dependent contraction of diabetic aorta is not caused by a defect in the Ca2+ release from intracellular stores.

the impaired Ca(2+)(i)-mobilization is one of the mechanisms for the reduced vascular reactivity in diabetic rat aortas.

the caffeine-induced transient contraction of the rat aorta is impaired in diabetes.
